title: TB1-11936
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Sri Lanka who seeks refugee protection pursuant to subsections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS

The complete story alleging the basis of the claimant's fears is captured in the Personal Information Form (PIF).2 The claimant alleges a fear in returning to Sri Lanka due to being suspected by authorities as being affiliated with LTTE, Liberation Tamil Tigers Eealam, a known terrorist group. The claimant was arrested, detained and beaten three separate times on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011, XXXX XXXX, 2011 and XXXX 2011. The claimant realized his life was at risk in XXXX 2011. The claimant departed Sri Lanka with his own passport and with the assistance of an agent and arrived in Canada via the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2011 and claimed refugee protection.

The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The panel also finds that should the claimant return to Sri Lanka that he would not be subjected personally to a risk to his life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. Further, on substantial grounds, there is no danger of torture.

On a balance of probabilities, the panel is willing to accept that the claimant is a citizen of Sri Lanka, who is Tamil in ethnicity, based on copies of his Sri Lankan birth certificate as seen in Exhibit R/A-2.

The determinative issue in this case is the credibility of the evidence as submitted. On the issue of credibility, the panel is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal case in Sellan3 which stated the following: Where the Board makes a general finding that the claimant lacks credibility, that determination is sufficient to dispose of the claim unless there is independent and credible documentary evidence in the record capable of supporting a positive disposition of the claim. The claimant bears the onus of demonstrating there was such evidence.

Furthermore, the Federal Court notes the following: The Board is in a much better position than a reviewing court to gage the credibility and plausibility of a refugee claimant's story. A credibility finding is not a finding of mixed fact and law. It is a finding of fact, pure and simple. Findings of fact made by the Board may only be interfered with by a reviewing court if the finding was made in a perverse or capricious manner or without regard for the material before it (see the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, paragraph 18.1(4)(d)). Indeed, it was Parliament's express intention that administrative fact-finding would command this high degree of deference (see Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12, [2009] S.C.J. No. 12 (QL) at paragraph 46). Thus, credibility findings of the Board are to be reviewed against the statutory standard of review provided for in paragraph 18.1(4)(d) of the Federal Courts Act (see Diabo v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 1772, [2004] F.C.J. No. 2168 (QL) at paragraph 3).

The evidence from the claimant resulting in his fear of return to Sri Lanka is due to being arrested, detained and beaten by the authorities due to the belief of the authorities that he is some how affiliated with the LTTE as the claimant played XXXX with a person, or in the same location of a person who is believed by the authorities to be associated with the LTTE. The officials apparently questioned the claimant about a person known as "XXXX" who is also believed to have some connection with the LTTE. The claimant would deny any relationship with "XXXX", other than being known to the claimant as a consequence of playing XXXX. The authorities, that being the army and CID did not believe the claimant and he continued to encounter problems until he realized his life was at risk in XXXX 2011 when he then made arrangements to leave the country.

The panel asked the claimant if he knows what information the authorities had to believe the claimant was somehow affiliated with the LTTE. The claimant indicated that he did not know where they obtained their information from. Based on the evidence, it appears the only known link is via the person known as "XXXX".

In trying to determine the likelihood of the claimant being suspected an affiliate of the LTTE, the panel considered the claimant's profile as a young Tamil male and whether there would be sufficient evidence that the claimant is involved or somehow supports the LTTE.

The evidence before this panel is replete with scathing reports about how government officials can be brutal towards persons it believes is involved with the LTTE. The panel notes the following from item 2.134 of the index: The aftermath of Sri Lanka's quarter century-long civil war, which ended in May 2009 with the defeat of the separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), continued to dominate events in 2011. In April United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon released a report by a panel of experts that concluded that both government forces and the LTTE conducted military operations "with flagrant disregard for the protection, rights, welfare and lives of civilians and failed to respect the norms of international law." The panel recommended the establishment of an international investigative mechanism. Sri Lankan officials responded by vilifying the report and the panel members. The government has failed to conduct credible investigations into alleged war crimes by security forces, dismissing the overwhelming body of evidence as LTTE propaganda. The government's Lessons Learnt and Reconciliation Commission (LLRC), characterized as a national accountability mechanism, is deeply flawed, does not meet international standards for such commissions, and has failed to systematically inquire into alleged abuses. Despite the end of the formal state of emergency, the government also continues to hold several thousand people initially detained under the emergency regulations. Many have been held for years without trial, in violation of international law. The government has so far refused to even publish lists of those detained. The government has gradually released many, but not all, of the more than 11,000 suspected LTTE members detained at the end of the war and sent to so-called rehabilitation centers. The government denied detainees important due process guarantees, such as access to legal counsel, and thousands spent two years or more in detention. There are reports that some people released from the rehabilitation centers were harassed by security forces after they returned home.

The claimant was asked by the panel whether he was in any way affiliated with the LTTE. He responded in the negative. The claimant essentially has no ties with the LTTE. The claimant apparently was the only one questioned in XXXX 2010 and in XXXX 2011. The claimant did though hear that 2 others were questioned after XXXX 2011 but he had no information about their circumstances.

If and only if the claimant played cricket with someone who apparently has some connection or is believed to have some connection with the LTTE, it is difficult to believe that the claimant was able to continue working in a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX from XXXX 2010 until XXXX 2011 given such interests in him by the authorities. The panel does not believe his evidence and makes a negative credibility finding as a result.

The claimant was asked when he realized that his life was at risk. The claimant responded that he realized that his life was at risk in XXXX 2011 when he was last detained, beaten and tortured by the police. The claimant alleges he was beaten with pipes, with the hands of the authorities and suffocated while in detention for three days and then released. Again, if the claimant was such an interest to the authorities as alleged where he suffered, the panel does not believe the claimant would be released after each subsequent arrest and detention if he was truly suspected to be a LTTE affiliated. The panel also finds it difficult to believe that the claimant would then return to work for two more months until he was able to leave the country. The panel makes another negative credibility finding as a consequence.

Furthermore, the claimant testified that after his detention and release in XXXX 2011, he was required to provide the authorities with information about "XXXX", the other person the authorities were interested in and do so within one month of release or he would be killed. There is no indication the claimant gave the authorities information about "XXXX", which would allow him to avoid being killed by the authorities while working and living in the country for an additional 2 months before leaving. The panel does not believe his evidence in this regard and makes a negative credibility finding.

The panel wishes to note item 13.15 of the index which provides some qualitative information about persons suspected of being LTTE affiliates or supporters. The document states: The methods for purging the "hidden" LTTE members who the government believes are still at large consist of "surveillance, arbitrary arrests and random check[s]," explains the Adjunct Professor (13 Jan. 2011). The second academic contacted by the Research Directorate, a York University law professor who is also a member of the advisory council of the Sri Lanka Campaign for Peace and Justice, somewhat similarly reports that Tamils throughout the country, particularly young Tamil men in the north or east, are being arrested and detained on suspicion of LTTE affiliation, a practice he describes as akin to "'ethnic' or 'racial' profiling" (Professor 20 Jan. 2011). The senior army officer reportedly told The New Yorker reporter that the army is building large military camps in the north and gathering intelligence with the help of spies in the Tamil population and electronic surveillance systems (The New Yorker 17 Jan. 2011, 49). The result of the government's efforts to find suspected Tigers is that screening is not limited to the IDP camps (Senior Research Fellow 28 Dec. 2010; Research Fellow 30 Dec. 2010). As the law professor explains, the government believes that "quite a number" of prominent LTTE figures remain at large and so is "very much on the look-out" for them (20 Jan. 2011). With the government still concerned with separating LTTE cadres from Tamil citizens, says the Senior Research Fellow, it is carrying out its screening in "residential areas all over the country" (28 Dec. 2010). According to the Research Fellow, screening is also being carried out at the airport (30 Dec. 2010). The law professor similarly says that he has it on good authority that the government is using "captured LTTE leaders as spotters at both the passport office in Colombo and at the airport" (20 Jan. 2011). He reports that the government is "routinely 'interview[ing]'" returned Tamil asylum seekers and, on what is "likely minimal standard[s]," arresting and detaining any who are suspected of being affiliated with the LTTE (Professor 20 Jan. 2011). He adds that Tamils flying into the Colombo airport who are not failed asylum claimants or deportees are also being "randomly screened and interrogated" (ibid.). Information corroborating the law professor's statement about the treatment of Tamils at the Colombo airport was not found among the sources consulted by the Research Directorate.

Given what the government does to locate suspected LTTE affiliates as well as using persons as spies, the panel asked the claimant how he was able to leave XXXX in the Northeastern area of the country to Colombo which is in the southern west location of the country. The claimant indicated that he traveled in a van as a passenger with his father and the driver to Colombo where they passed through approximately 5-6 checkpoints. The doors were opened when stopped and the claimant was seen but no questions were directed to him from the authorities.

Even if the driver who, according to the claimant spoke Sinhala to the authorities, given the alleged suspicion that the claimant is affiliated somehow with the LTTE, it would be reasonable to expect that the claimant would have been questioned or interrogated by the authorities to ensure his identity whether or not he had problems with the authorities in the past. This is not the case and it is difficult to believe this is so given the human rights violations committed by the authorities with a view of locating suspected LTTE affiliates. Again, the panel does not believe that the claimant is in any way of interest to the authorities or was believed to be a suspected LTTE affiliate. The panel makes another negative credibility finding as a result.

Furthermore, the panel asked the claimant how he was able to obtain a passport issued in his own name in XXXX 2011 which is valid until XXXX 2021, given his alleged problems. The claimant indicated that he does not know how the agent obtained it for him. If the claimant is remotely on the radar of the authorities, regardless as to who applied for and obtained the passport, the panel does not see it credible, nor does the panel believe that the claimant would have been able to obtain a passport and successfully leave the country via the airport in Colombo with his passport. The panel makes a negative credibility finding as a result.

The claimant was asked if he had any information from his family about his situation today. The claimant stated that the authorities went to his home approximately 7-8 times asking about him. The claimant's father and or other relatives indicated that the claimant left XXXX. The authorities allegedly stated that "since he has connection to XXXX, we are looking for your son."

The panel has difficulty believing the claimant has any connection with "XXXX" or is suspected by the authorities of being affiliated with the LTTE in a big or small way. If that was truly the case, the claimant would not likely be able to continue working after his alleged problems, would not likely be able to pass through 5-6 checkpoints undiscovered and would not likely be able to successfully obtain a passport in his own name in XXXX of 2011 and likely leave the country with the said passport if he was in fact wanted or of interest to the authorities in some way. Also, there is no credible indication that the claimant's family has suffered acts of persecution due to the claimant's situation and the claimant being lucky enough to successfully leave the country. The panel does not believe the evidence as presented and makes a negative credibility finding.

In counsel's submissions, he indicates that the claimant fits a profile similar to many Sri Lankan Tamil males who have been accepted in Canada as refugees. It was also stated that the claimant is not a person that is of important interest to the authorities, but of some interest which would put the claimant's life at risk.

It is known that each case is assessed on its own merits and therefore it would not be appropriate to make a finding in favour of the claimant on this premise alone. Many factors have to be addressed to properly adjudicate claims as to their well foundedness of persecution. Based on the totality of the evidence, inclusive of counsel's submissions, the panel has not been so persuaded that the claimant is of particular interest to the authorities and therefore has a well founded fear of persecution or that his life is at risk pursuant to section 97 of the Act based on what is stated previously in these reasons.

At this juncture, the panel wishes to comment on the psychological assessment as referenced in Exhibit C-2 from Dr. XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2012. The panel notes that the claimant was assessed by the said doctor on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012. The information contained in the report comes from the claimant with evidence similar as that of the Personal Information Form. After one known interview, the psychologist summarizes that the claimant is presented with a "Major Depressive Episode and Post Traumatic Stress Disorder."

The information contained in the psychological assessment is not persuasive evidence for this panel that the doctor is in any position to state categorically that the claimant before it is suffering from "Major Depressive Episode and Post Traumatic Stress Disorder" as a result of the problems allegedly faced in Sri Lanka.

As stated in Rokni,6 a psychiatric/psychological letter submitted as evidence "cannot possibly serve as a cure-all for any and all deficiencies in a claimant's testimony". The court reiterated its position in Danailov,7 with respect to the assessment of a physician's evidence and the question of the assessment of credibility. It was stated "that opinion evidence is only as valid as the truth of the facts on which it is based." The panel finds that, although the claimant identified may be suffering from "Major Depressive Episode and Post Traumatic Stress Disorder" and or other mental illnesses, this may or may not be related to the problems described by the claimant in his evidence. The panel therefore gives little weight to the psychological assessment submitted for the panel's review.

In Li,8 the Federal Court stated "pursuant to subsection 97(1) there must be persuasive evidence, that is on a balance of probabilities establishing the facts on which a claimant relies, to say that he or she faces a substantial danger of being tortured on his or her return. Second, the danger or risk must be such that it is more likely than not that he or she would be tortured or subjected to other cruel or other degrading treatments." This is not the case in this claim.

In Bouaouni,9 the Federal Court stated "a claim under section 97 must be evaluated with respect to all the relevant considerations and with a view to the country's human rights record." In evaluating this claim under section 97 and considering the human rights record of Sri Lanka, the panel has not been persuaded that the claimant would face a substantial danger of being tortured, or that the risk and/or danger is such that it would be more likely than not that the claimant would be tortured or subjected to cruel or other degrading treatments, based on what has already been mentioned earlier in these reasons.

Therefore, after a thorough review of this case, the claimant has failed to meet his onus that he has a well founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground or that he is in need of protection in a clear and convincing fashion as this case is being assessed, forward looking.

Having considered all the evidence, the panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee as he has not established that there is a reasonable chance or serious possibility that he would be persecuted for a Convention ground or there would be a risk to his life or he would be subjected to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should he be required to return to Sri Lanka in a forward looking analysis. On substantial grounds, there is insufficient grounds to establish danger of torture should the claimant return to Sri Lanka given the panel does not believe this claim as alleged. The panel rejects this claim pursuant to both sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. (signed) "K. Dickenson" K.
